title: Paid editorial content not made clear (advertorial)

jurisdiction.name: European Union (applies where consumers in the EU are reached)

instrument: Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC, consolidated text of 27.09.2026
binding_note: A directive that each Member State applies through its national law. Annex I lists practices that are unfair in all circumstances. The same single list applies in all Member States. It covers practices from a business to consumers, so the party must be a trader.

in_force.note: Original Annex I point, in the 2005 text and unchanged in the consolidated version of 27.09.2026.

sources.publisher: Publications Office of the European Union (Cellar), consolidated text
sources.note: EUR-Lex answered scripted requests with an empty 202 challenge, so the same document was read from the Publications Office repository that serves EUR-Lex. Consolidated version 02005L0029-20260927, the latest listed in Cellar on the retrieval date (earlier: 20220528). The consolidated text states it has no legal effect; the Official Journal texts are authentic.

quotes.text: Using editorial content in the media to promote a product where a trader has paid for the promotion without making that clear in the content or by images or sounds clearly identifiable by the consumer (advertorial).

elements.label: Content presented as editorial or ordinary content is used to promote a product
elements.note: Whether a social media post counts as "editorial content in the media" is a legal question for courts.

elements.label: A trader paid for the promotion
elements.note: Shown for labelled posts, where the poster disclosed the payment. Payment for unlabelled posts sits in records off the page.

elements.label: The payment is not made clear in the content or by images or sounds the consumer can clearly identify
elements.note: CMMNS checks for the platform's own paid label. A disclosure can also take other forms.

does_not_prove: For unlabelled posts, elements B and C rest on look-alike evidence. A match compares visible elements with the published text. Courts and consumer authorities decide whether the rule was broken.
